edges.title: A folk poem interrupts the symphony

works.to: Urlicht; Symphony No. 2, movement IV

edges.claim: Mahler set Urlicht, a poem from Des Knaben Wunderhorn, before placing it between the Second Symphony’s scherzo and finale. After three instrumental movements, an alto enters with an intimate appeal for release.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Urlicht and the Second Symphony

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Urlicht
sources.locator: Poem and composition history

edges.title: The fish sermon loses its words

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt
works.to: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt; Symphony No. 2, movement III

edges.claim: In Mahler’s Wunderhorn song, Saint Anthony preaches to the fish. They listen attentively, then carry on exactly as before. Mahler takes the song’s music into the Second Symphony’s scherzo, where the sermon circles on without words.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Fischpredigt and Symphony No. 2

edges.title: A child’s heaven becomes the destination

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Das himmlische Leben
works.to: Symphony No. 4, finale

edges.claim: Mahler composed Das himmlische Leben in 1892, years before the Fourth Symphony, then reorchestrated it as the finale. The symphony ends with this older song: a soprano describing a child’s heaven of food, saints and music.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Das himmlische Leben, 1892 and 1899–1900

edges.title: Bruckner’s Third passes through four hands

works.to: Piano-duet arrangement, 1878–1880

edges.claim: Mahler and Rudolf Krzyzanowski prepared a piano-duet arrangement of [[bruckner]]’s Third Symphony, compressing the 1877 orchestral score into four hands at one keyboard.
edges.note: The precise division of work between Mahler and Krzyzanowski remains uncertain.

sources.title: Paul Banks: Gustav Mahler, arrangements
sources.locator: Bruckner, Symphony No. 3: 1878–1880

sources.title: MusicWeb International: Bruckner Third, Mahler/Krzyzanowski arrangement
sources.locator: Attribution and 1877 version

edges.title: Parsifal heard at Bayreuth

works.to: Mahler’s Bayreuth visit and letter to Fritz Löhr

edges.claim: At Bayreuth in 1883, Mahler heard [[wagner]]’s Parsifal under Hermann Levi. He wrote to Fritz Löhr about the experience.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Gustav Mahler in Bayreuth
sources.locator: 1883 visit; Parsifal and the letter to Fritz Löhr

edges.title: Bruder Martin walks into a funeral

works.from: Bruder Martin / Frère Jacques, traditional round
works.to: Symphony No. 1, movement III, opening canon

edges.claim: Over the timpani’s tread, the First Symphony’s third movement introduces Bruder Martin, the round also known as Frère Jacques, in D minor and builds a canon from it. Mahler adds a small F–E quaver turn. Minor-mode versions of the round were already circulating in Austria.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 1, introduction
sources.locator: Third movement: Bruder Martin and Austrian minor-mode tradition

sources.locator: 1898 score facsimile, opening of movement III

edges.title: Jean Paul lends Mahler a title

works.to: Symphony No. 1: Hamburg programme, 1893

edges.claim: For the First Symphony’s Hamburg performance in 1893, Mahler borrowed the name Titan from Jean Paul’s novel. He later withdrew both programme and title, leaving a four-movement symphony.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 1, introduction
sources.locator: Hamburg 1893 and withdrawal of the programme

edges.title: Reading the symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov

works.to: Symphonies Nos. 3 and 4

edges.claim: Mahler admired Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov. Celeste Belknap reads his Third and Fourth Symphonies alongside the novel, bringing its questions of faith and childhood to bear on the Fourth’s closing vision of heaven.
edges.note: Belknap proposes structural and philosophical parallels. Their role in Mahler’s actual compositional decisions remains unproven.

sources.title: Celeste Belknap: Brothers in Philosophy: Interpreting Mahler’s Third and Fourth Symphonies through a Dostoevskian Lens
sources.locator: 2021 thesis abstract; full thesis not opened

edges.title: Rott and Mahler dance the Ländler

works.to: Symphony No. 1, scherzo; comparison with Symphony No. 5

edges.claim: The Ländler-like scherzo of Hans Rott’s E-major Symphony has close cousins in Mahler’s First and Fifth. Mahler knew Rott as a fellow student, later praised his music and borrowed the symphony’s score in 1900.
edges.note: Mahler’s access to Rott’s score before composing his First Symphony remains uncertain. The documented loan of 1900 comes later; the edge year dates Mahler’s work.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Hans Rott
sources.locator: E-major Symphony; scherzo comparisons; Mahler’s 1900 score loan

edges.title: The garrison town enters the orchestra

works.from: Military bands and street music in Iglau
works.to: Mahler’s childhood listening; later marches and fanfares

edges.claim: Mahler grew up in Iglau, a Bohemian garrison town where military bands sounded alongside church bells, synagogue music and street musicians. Michael Tilson Thomas traces the marches and fanfares of Mahler’s orchestra back to those childhood streets.

sources.title: San Francisco Symphony / PBS: Mahler’s Origins
sources.locator: Iglau childhood soundscape

edges.title: Bach on the composing-hut desk

works.to: Mahler’s Bach study during the Hamburg years

edges.claim: Mahler subscribed to the Bach-Gesellschaft edition during his Hamburg years. Natalie Bauer-Lechner and Alma Mahler remembered his sustained study of [[bach]]; Bach’s scores accompanied him even to his composing retreat.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Mahler and Bach
sources.locator: Hamburg subscription, 1891–1897; Bauer-Lechner and Alma recollections

edges.title: Two Bach suites become one programme

works.to: Suite aus den Orchesterwerken von J. S. Bach

edges.claim: Mahler assembled a performing suite from movements of [[bach]]’s Second and Third Orchestral Suites. He selected and rearranged the movements for his own concerts.

sources.title: Paul Banks: Gustav Mahler, arrangements
sources.locator: Bach suite, 1910

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Mahler and Bach
sources.locator: Suite assembled from Orchestral Suites Nos. 2 and 3

edges.title: China reaches Mahler through several translators

works.to: Das Lied von der Erde

edges.claim: Mahler drew the texts of Das Lied von der Erde from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte, combining seven poems into six songs. The Chinese poems had reached Bethge through earlier European translations, including those of Judith Gautier and the Marquis d’Hervey-Saint-Denys; he made German paraphrases of them.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Das Lied von der Erde, introduction
sources.locator: Bethge’s anthology and the European translation chain

edges.title: Rückert’s private grief becomes five songs

works.from: Kindertotenlieder, poems written after the deaths of two children
works.to: Kindertotenlieder, 1901–1904

edges.claim: Friedrich Rückert wrote his Kindertotenlieder after losing two children in 1833–34. Mahler selected five poems and set them in 1901–04. His own daughter Maria died in 1907.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Friedrich Rückert
sources.locator: Rückert’s bereavements and Mahler’s five settings, 1901–1904

edges.title: A memorial service unlocks the finale

works.to: Symphony No. 2, finale

edges.claim: At Hans von Bülow’s memorial service in 1894, Mahler heard Klopstock’s resurrection hymn and found the words with which to begin his Second Symphony’s finale. He joined part of the hymn to verses of his own.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Hans von Bülow
sources.locator: Memorial-service account and the Second Symphony’s finale

edges.title: Faust answers Veni creator spiritus

works.to: Symphony No. 8, Part II

edges.claim: The Eighth Symphony begins with the Latin hymn Veni creator spiritus and ends with the closing scene of Goethe’s Faust II. Music from the opening invocation returns in Goethe’s final ascent.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 8, introduction
sources.locator: Two texts and shared thematic material

edges.title: Zarathustra sings at midnight

works.to: Symphony No. 3, movement IV

edges.claim: After three instrumental movements, Mahler’s Third Symphony brings in an alto singing Nietzsche’s midnight poem from Also sprach Zarathustra. The orchestra grows sparse and slow around the solitary voice contemplating sorrow and eternity.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 3, movement IV
sources.locator: Nietzsche’s Midnight Song and the alto setting

edges.title: Mahler’s orchestra behind Berg’s three pieces

works.to: Three Pieces for Orchestra, Op. 6

edges.claim: Mark DeVoto hears Mahler’s Ninth behind [[berg]]’s Three Pieces for Orchestra, written in 1914–15. The central Reigen turns through dances including a Ländler; the final Marsch drives the orchestra into a destructive march.

sources.title: Mark DeVoto / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Berg, Three Pieces for Orchestra
sources.locator: Mahler’s Ninth; Reigen and Marsch; composition in 1914–1915

edges.title: Teenage Britten hears Mahler’s Fourth

works.to: Britten’s diary; early orchestral work including Plymouth Town

edges.claim: The teenage [[britten]] heard Mahler’s Fourth at a London Prom in September 1930. His diary mingles impatience at its length with admiration for its beauty. David Matthews traces the encounter, and Britten’s subsequent purchase of the Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen score, into the orchestra of Plymouth Town.

sources.title: David Matthews: London, Royal College of Music: Britten’s Plymouth Town, Tempo 58/230 (2004)
sources.locator: pp. 57–58, Britten’s 1930 diary and 1931 score purchase

edges.title: Zverev’s household was also a conservatory

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow training, from 1885

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff entered Nikolai Zverev’s Moscow household as a piano pupil in 1885. Its musical gatherings also brought him into contact with [[tchaikovsky]], so the teacher provided both intensive pianistic training and access to the professional circle in which the young composer was first heard.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Zverev’s household and musical soirées, 1885 onwards

edges.title: A cousin takes over the piano lessons

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s senior Moscow studies

edges.claim: In 1888 Rachmaninoff entered the senior course at the Moscow Conservatory and began piano lessons with his cousin Alexander Siloti. Alongside them came composition with Arensky and counterpoint with Taneyev.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Senior studies from 1888

edges.title: Tchaikovsky recommends advanced counterpoint

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow Conservatory studies

edges.claim: On [[tchaikovsky]]’s recommendation, Rachmaninoff studied advanced counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev at the Moscow Conservatory: the craft of making independent voices work together.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Taneyev and Tchaikovsky’s recommendation

edges.title: Arensky teaches the composer’s working tools

works.from: Anton Arensky’s harmony, instrumentation and composition classes
works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow Conservatory studies

edges.claim: In the senior course at the Moscow Conservatory, Rachmaninoff studied composition with Anton Arensky. The lessons included harmony and instrumentation; Taneyev taught him counterpoint and Siloti piano.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Arensky’s subjects in the senior course

edges.title: Tchaikovsky champions the graduation opera

works.from: Tchaikovsky’s support and proposed Iolanta double bill
works.to: Aleko, composed 1892; Bolshoi premiere, 1893

edges.claim: [[tchaikovsky]] publicly praised Rachmaninoff’s graduation opera Aleko. He attended its Bolshoi première in 1893 and proposed a double bill with his own Iolanta.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: December 1892 interview; Aleko premiere, 27 April/9 May 1893; Iolanta proposal

edges.title: A memorial trio answers a memorial trio

works.from: Piano Trio in A minor, Op. 50, in memory of Nikolai Rubinstein
works.to: Trio élégiaque No. 2 in D minor, Op. 9

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff completed his Second Trio élégiaque in December 1893, mourning [[tchaikovsky]]. The choice of a large piano trio followed his patron’s example: Tchaikovsky had written his own trio in memory of Nikolai Rubinstein.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Trio élégiaque No. 2, completion 15/27 December 1893

edges.title: Grieg provides a concerto starting point

works.from: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16
works.to: Piano Concerto No. 1 in F-sharp minor, Op. 1, original version

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff used Grieg’s concerto as a model for the original version of his First Piano Concerto in 1891. He returned to his student score in 1917 and revised it extensively.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: First Piano Concerto, Grieg model and later revision

edges.title: Dies irae crosses the dark water

works.to: The Isle of the Dead, Op. 29

edges.claim: The medieval Dies irae crosses Rachmaninoff’s The Isle of the Dead in fragments and fuller statements. Böcklin supplied the island; the chant brings its own memory of death to the music.

sources.title: Timothy Judd: Rachmaninov’s Isle of the Dead: A Tone Poem in Black and White
sources.locator: Dies irae fragments and statements

edges.title: The death chant interrupts Paganini

works.to: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, Op. 43, variation VII

edges.claim: In Variation VII of the Paganini Rhapsody, the piano plays Dies irae. Bassoons and pizzicato cellos answer with fragments of Paganini’s theme: the death chant and the violin caprice now share the same music.

sources.title: Calvin Dotsey / Houston Symphony: Rachmaninoff’s Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini
sources.locator: 7 March 2025; variation VII

edges.title: Dies irae returns in the last dance

works.to: Symphonic Dances, Op. 45, movement III

edges.claim: The final Symphonic Dance repeatedly invokes Dies irae, returning to a melody Rachmaninoff had already used in The Isle of the Dead and the Paganini Rhapsody. It is set against music recalled from his own All-Night Vigil, turning the movement into an encounter between a Western death chant and his Russian sacred repertory.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Rachmaninoff, Symphonic Dances
sources.locator: Movement III: Dies irae and All-Night Vigil quotation

edges.title: Old chant becomes a choral orchestra

works.to: All-Night Vigil, Op. 37, including Nos. 8 and 12

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff built parts of his All-Night Vigil around inherited Orthodox chants. In No. 8, altos and basses carry the Znamenny melody in octaves; No. 12 draws on the same chant tradition.

sources.title: David Bray: Rachmaninoff Vespers, Signum SIGCD054 booklet
sources.locator: Booklet pp. 4–7; Znamenny tradition and movements 8 and 12

edges.title: The Vigil’s Alleluia survives in exile

works.from: All-Night Vigil, Op. 37, No. 9, based on Znamenny chant
works.to: Symphonic Dances, Op. 45, movement III, coda

edges.claim: Near the end of the Symphonic Dances, Rachmaninoff recalls the ninth movement of his All-Night Vigil and marks the passage with an Alleluia indication. The Russian sacred melody reaches the orchestral work through his own earlier choral setting: it is both inherited chant and self-quotation.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Rachmaninoff, Symphonic Dances
sources.locator: Final movement’s quotation of Vigil No. 9 and Alleluia marking

edges.title: Böcklin’s island becomes a symphonic poem

works.from: Die Toteninsel / Isle of the Dead, series of paintings
works.to: The Isle of the Dead, Op. 29

edges.claim: A black-and-white reproduction of Böcklin’s Isle of the Dead prompted Rachmaninoff’s tone poem. When he later saw the painting in colour, he found it less compelling. In the music, a recurring 5/8 carries the imagined crossing towards the island.
edges.note: The illustration shows the Basel version of the painting. The exact reproduction Rachmaninoff saw remains unidentified here.

sources.locator: 1907 reproduction encounter and the tone poem

edges.title: Chopin’s miniature becomes twenty-two variations

works.from: Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20
works.to: Variations on a Theme of Chopin, Op. 22

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff took [[chopin]]’s C-minor Prelude as the theme for twenty-two piano variations, written in 1902–03. The paired excerpts show the upper voice of Chopin’s opening chords and Rachmaninoff’s restatement.

edges.title: The pianist writes inside Liszt’s rhapsody

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s cadenza, documented in a concert programme of 23 January 1919

edges.claim: At Carnegie Hall in January 1919, Rachmaninoff played [[liszt]]’s Second Hungarian Rhapsody with a cadenza of his own. The programme names his addition: the pianist had written himself into the piece.

edges.title: Paganini’s theme arrives after its first variation

works.from: Caprice No. 24 in A minor, Op. 1
works.to: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, Op. 43

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff built his Rhapsody on Paganini’s Twenty-fourth Caprice, putting a skeletal first variation before the theme itself. In the eighteenth variation he turns the theme upside down and into the major, and the long singing melody emerges.

edges.title: Poe’s bells arrive through Balmont

works.from: The Bells, in Konstantin Balmont’s Russian adaptation
works.to: The Bells, Op. 35

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s choral symphony The Bells sets Konstantin Balmont’s free Russian adaptation of Poe. Its four movements pass through sleigh bells, wedding bells, alarm bells and funeral bells. Balmont brings death into the poem earlier than Poe does.

sources.locator: Poe, Balmont and the four-movement text

edges.title: Mahler rehearses Rachmaninoff’s Third

works.to: Piano Concerto No. 3, January 1910 performances

edges.claim: In New York in January 1910, [[mahler]] conducted Rachmaninoff as soloist in the Third Piano Concerto, following its première under Walter Damrosch. Rachmaninoff later remembered the pains Mahler took over rehearsing the new score.

sources.title: New Mexico Philharmonic: Rachmaninoff & Ravel programme notes
sources.locator: Third Piano Concerto: Damrosch premiere and Mahler performances

edges.title: Fauré’s classroom hears the young Ravel

works.to: Ravel’s studies; early Sonata for violin and piano

edges.claim: Ravel entered [[faure]]’s composition class in 1897. His early single-movement violin sonata belongs to those student years; Bru Zane hears Fauré’s chamber music behind it.
edges.note: Bru Zane dates a classroom performance to 1897–98 but treats it as probable.

edges.title: Gédalge teaches the contrapuntal craft

works.to: Ravel’s Conservatoire-period training

edges.claim: Alongside his work in Fauré’s composition class, Ravel took private counterpoint lessons with André Gédalge.

sources.title: Maurice Ravel: biography and Conservatoire studies
sources.locator: 1897 studies with Fauré and private counterpoint with Gédalge

edges.title: Chabrier behind the grotesque serenade

works.to: Sérénade grotesque

edges.claim: Looking back in his autobiographical account, Ravel named Chabrier as the model behind his early piano piece Sérénade grotesque.

sources.locator: 14 July 2025; Ravel’s retrospective account of the two early pieces

edges.title: Ravel names Satie as an early model

works.to: Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer

edges.claim: Ravel’s autobiographical sketch names [[satie]] as an influence on his early Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer.

works.to: Pavane pour une infante défunte, original piano version

edges.claim: In the Pavane’s calmly held dissonances and unexpected bass notes, Peter Jost hears a kinship with [[satie]]’s early piano writing. The resemblance lies beneath Ravel’s tune, in the accompaniment.
edges.note: Jost proposes a harmonic resemblance. Whether Ravel consciously drew on a particular Satie passage remains uncertain.

edges.title: Ravel takes compositional advice from Poe

works.from: The Philosophy of Composition, through Baudelaire’s translations
works.to: Ravel’s account of his compositional method

edges.claim: Ravel named Poe’s The Philosophy of Composition as a guide to his own work. Emily Kilpatrick connects that reading with his insistence on deliberate construction and originality.

edges.title: Pictures gains a saxophone and an orchestra

works.from: Pictures at an Exhibition, piano suite, 1874
works.to: Pictures at an Exhibition, orchestration, 1922

edges.claim: Serge Koussevitzky commissioned Ravel’s orchestration of [[mussorgsky]]’s piano Pictures at an Exhibition, first performed in Paris in October 1922. The trumpet’s opening Promenade and the alto saxophone of The Old Castle are Ravel’s instrumental decisions: the melodies and suite belong to Mussorgsky, while the familiar orchestral colours belong to the arranger.

edges.title: An old French suite mourns modern soldiers

works.from: Couperin and the French keyboard-suite tradition
works.to: Le Tombeau de Couperin, piano suite, 1914–1917

edges.claim: Le Tombeau de Couperin salutes the French keyboard tradition of [[couperin]] while mourning men killed in the First World War. Each movement has its own memorial dedication. The Toccata remembers Joseph de Marliave; his widow, Marguerite Long, gave the complete suite’s première in 1919.

works.from: Spanish songs sung by Ravel’s mother
works.to: Ravel’s Spanish musical world, including Rapsodie espagnole

edges.claim: Spain began at home for Ravel: his mother sang Spanish songs to him. That childhood music helps explain the recurring Spanish subjects of his work, including Rapsodie espagnole.

edges.title: The Trio sways in three-two-three

works.to: Piano Trio in A minor, movement I

edges.claim: The first movement of Ravel’s Piano Trio groups its eight quavers as 3 + 2 + 3. The short middle group gives the bar its uneven sway, a rhythm drawn from Basque dance.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Beaux Arts Trio Farewell Concert, Ravel Trio programme note
sources.locator: Ravel Trio: first movement’s 8/8 grouped 3 + 2 + 3

edges.title: Ravel’s Blues predates the American tour

works.to: Sonata for violin and piano, movement II, Blues

edges.claim: Ravel had already written the Blues movement of his Violin Sonata in 1927 when he set out for America the following year and met [[gershwin|George Gershwin]].

edges.title: Gershwin plays at Ravel’s birthday party

works.from: Rhapsody in Blue and The Man I Love
works.to: Ravel’s New York encounter with Gershwin, 7 March 1928

edges.claim: Éva Gauthier held a party in New York for Ravel’s birthday on 7 March 1928. [[gershwin]] sat at the piano and played, including Rhapsody in Blue and The Man I Love.

sources.title: Jack Zimmerman / Chicago Symphony Orchestra: Fascinatin’ Rhythm: When Ravel met Gershwin

edges.title: Russian orchestral colour reaches Paris

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s music at the Paris Exposition
works.to: Ravel’s youthful orchestral listening

edges.claim: At the Paris Exposition of 1889, the young Ravel heard Russian music associated with [[rimsky-korsakov]]. His interest in the Russian orchestra dates back to that encounter.

sources.locator: 1889 Exposition: Rimsky-Korsakov and Russian music

edges.title: Gaspard renews Lisztian virtuosity

works.to: Gaspard de la nuit, especially Scarbo

edges.claim: Emily Kilpatrick places Gaspard de la nuit in [[liszt]]’s tradition of the virtuoso pianist-composer. In Scarbo, extreme demands on the hands bring the goblin’s antics to the keyboard.
edges.note: The Liszt connection is Kilpatrick’s interpretation of Ravel’s piano writing. A particular borrowed passage has not been identified.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, pp. 11–12: virtuoso tradition and Scarbo

edges.title: Scarbo aims beyond Islamey

works.to: Gaspard de la nuit: Scarbo

edges.claim: Ravel wanted Scarbo to be harder to play than Balakirev’s Islamey. Repeated notes and leaps make Bertrand’s elusive goblin a formidable opponent for the pianist.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, p. 11; Ravel’s Islamey ambition, citing Orenstein

edges.title: Three prose poems become piano scenes

works.from: Gaspard de la nuit: Ondine, Le Gibet and Scarbo
works.to: Gaspard de la nuit, three poems for piano

edges.claim: Ravel printed Aloysius Bertrand’s prose poems alongside the three movements of Gaspard de la nuit. The water spirit of Ondine speaks, the bell of Le Gibet tolls, and the goblin Scarbo disappears.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, pp. 10–15: Bertrand’s poems and the three movements

edges.title: Schubert lends two waltz titles

works.to: Valses nobles et sentimentales

edges.claim: Ravel took the name Valses nobles et sentimentales from [[schubert]]’s two waltz collections. The old titles sit over waltzes with Ravel’s abrasive harmonies.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, p. 4: Ravel’s statement about Schubert and the title

edges.title: Vaughan Williams comes to Paris for clarity

works.from: Ravel’s lessons in composition and orchestral craft
works.to: Vaughan Williams’s Paris study, 1907–1908

edges.claim: Ralph Vaughan Williams spent about three months studying with Ravel in Paris in 1907–08. Their surviving correspondence records lessons in clear writing and orchestral craft, with a Mozart minuet among the pieces on the desk.

sources.title: Tom Service: How Ravel helped Vaughan Williams find his voice
sources.locator: Paris lessons and British Library correspondence

edges.title: Rimsky’s crowded orchestration classroom

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s St Petersburg Conservatory orchestration classes
works.to: Prokofiev’s student training

edges.claim: Prokofiev studied orchestration in [[rimsky-korsakov]]’s crowded classes at the St Petersburg Conservatory. He disliked the conditions, as David Nice records in his biography.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 10, biography: 1906 entry

edges.title: Lyadov’s rules meet an impatient modernist

works.from: Anatoly Lyadov’s harmony and counterpoint teaching
works.to: Prokofiev’s St Petersburg Conservatory studies

edges.claim: Prokofiev found Anatoly Lyadov’s harmony and counterpoint lessons uninspiring. Lyadov, in turn, was alarmed by the traces of Scriabin in his pupil’s 1909 examination pieces.

sources.title: Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff, biography
sources.locator: Conservatory teachers and subjects

sources.locator: p. 10, 1906 and 1909 entries

edges.title: Conducting lessons plant the Classical Symphony

works.from: Nikolai Tcherepnin’s conducting classes and Haydn/Mozart study
works.to: Prokofiev’s training; Piano Concerto No. 1 dedication

edges.claim: Nikolai Tcherepnin taught Prokofiev conducting and encouraged his close study of Haydn and Mozart. Prokofiev dedicated his First Piano Concerto to him, while the Tcherepnin Society’s account connects those classical studies with the later conception of the Classical Symphony.

sources.title: Tcherepnin Society: Nikolai Tcherepnin biography
sources.locator: Prokofiev’s studies, concerto dedication and Classical Symphony

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 10, 1909; p. 19, Piano Concerto No. 1 dedication

edges.title: Glière visits the child composer at home

works.to: Prokofiev’s lessons at Sontsovka, 1902–1903

edges.claim: On Taneyev’s recommendation, Reinhold Glière came to Sontsovka to teach the young Prokofiev. They worked together for two summers before Prokofiev entered the St Petersburg Conservatory.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 10, 1902 entry

edges.title: Haydn’s orchestra, with modern wrong turns

works.from: Haydn’s symphonic style and orchestral practice
works.to: Symphony No. 1 in D major, Op. 25, Classical

edges.claim: Writing his Classical Symphony in 1916–17, Prokofiev wondered how [[haydn]] might compose in the modern world. He kept the compact orchestra and four movements, threw in abrupt turns of harmony, and put a gavotte where Haydn usually put a minuet.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Prokofiev, Symphony No. 1

edges.title: Diaghilev rejects one ballet and orders another

works.to: Ala et Lolly; Chout; Scythian Suite

edges.claim: Diaghilev commissioned Ala et Lolly after meeting Prokofiev in 1914, rejected it, then ordered the Russian folk-tale ballet Chout. Prokofiev rescued the rejected music for his Scythian Suite.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 11, 1914–1916 chronology

edges.title: A piano audition turns into a quarrel

works.to: The Love for Three Oranges and Prokofiev’s response

edges.claim: At a 1922 piano presentation of The Love for Three Oranges for Diaghilev, [[stravinsky]] objected to the opera and quarrelled with Prokofiev. The two had once sat at the piano together to play Petrushka.

sources.title: Sergei Prokofiev: life abroad and the Stravinsky quarrel
sources.locator: Life abroad: June 1922 audition and quarrel

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 11, 1915 Petrushka duet

edges.title: Film follows music; music follows film

works.to: Alexander Nevsky film score; concert cantata, Op. 78

edges.claim: For Alexander Nevsky, Eisenstein sometimes shaped images to Prokofiev’s music; elsewhere Prokofiev composed to the images. In 1939 he recast the previous year’s film score as a concert cantata.

sources.title: University Musical Society: Alexander Nevsky, 22 March 2025
sources.locator: Eisenstein–Prokofiev working methods and concert cantata

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 14, 1938–1939 chronology

edges.title: Romeo and Juliet nearly survived the ballet

works.to: Romeo and Juliet, ballet, Op. 64

edges.claim: In the first plan for Prokofiev’s 1935 ballet, Romeo arrived in time and both lovers survived. The authors eventually restored Shakespeare’s tragic ending.

sources.title: Jim Svejda / Los Angeles Philharmonic: Romeo and Juliet, complete ballet, Op. 64
sources.locator: 1935 composition and the abandoned happy ending

edges.title: Prokofiev’s Onegin waits for a cancelled production

works.to: Eugene Onegin, incidental music, Op. 71

edges.claim: Prokofiev wrote Eugene Onegin music for Alexander Tairov’s planned stage production in 1936, setting spoken voices against an orchestra. The production was cancelled; the score survived.

sources.title: Wise Music Classical: Prokofiev, Eugene Onegin, Op. 71
sources.locator: 1936 Tairov commission, spoken forces and cancelled production

edges.title: Christian Science enters the composer’s own account

works.from: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures; Christian Science teaching
works.to: Prokofiev’s diaries and 31 January 1933 letter to Eve Crain

edges.claim: Prokofiev’s diaries record his reading of Mary Baker Eddy’s Science and Health and his interest in Christian Science from 1924. In a letter of 1933, he connected the faith with his work as a composer.

sources.title: Mary Baker Eddy Library: From the Collections: Sergei Prokofiev and Christian Science
sources.locator: 1924 diary entries; facsimile and transcription of 31 January 1933 letter

edges.title: Dostoevsky’s obsession becomes an opera

works.to: The Gambler, opera, Op. 24, 1915–1917; revised 1927–1928

edges.claim: Prokofiev made Dostoevsky’s The Gambler into an opera in 1915–17. The first planned production fell through while he was still in Russia, and a decade later he revised the score.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: pp. 4 and 11–13, Dostoevsky source, composition and abandoned production

edges.title: Tolstoy’s invasion meets a second invasion

works.to: War and Peace, opera, Op. 91, begun 1941

edges.claim: After the German invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, Prokofiev turned to Tolstoy’s War and Peace. He and Mira Mendelson chose scenes from the novel for an opera that he would revise repeatedly.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: pp. 4 and 14–16, Tolstoy source and 1941–1953 chronology

edges.title: Rachmaninoff’s Corelli theme is the older Folia

works.from: Corelli, Sonata Op. 5 No. 12, Follia (1700), inherited theme
works.to: Variations on a Theme of Corelli, Op. 42 (1931)

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff composed his Variations on a Theme of Corelli in May and June 1931. The theme is the old Folia melody that Corelli had used for his Op. 5 finale.
edges.note: The route by which Rachmaninoff knew the Folia remains uncertain. Kreisler is often proposed as the intermediary; the critical discussion also points to Rachmaninoff’s familiarity with Liszt’s Rhapsodie espagnole.

sources.title: Norbert Gertsch, Henle: Corelli, La Folia and Rachmaninoff’s Variations, Op. 42
sources.locator: Rachmaninoff’s May–June 1931 composition, Folia ancestry, and uncertain Kreisler/Liszt transmission
